title: Israel is prepared to respond to Iranian attacks, says defence minister
summary:
Israel is prepared to respond to Iranian attacks, says defence minister

Israeli forces are prepared for a possible attack from Iran over the Jewish high holiday season which begins in mid-September, the country's defence minister said Wednesday.

"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," he told a conference hosted by Israeli news outlet Yedioth Ahronoth.

"But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively."

summary:

title: Iran war: Trump can continue the same failed policies - or shape a historic legacy
summary:
Iran war: Trump can continue the same failed policies - or shape a historic legacy

Submitted by Seyed Hossein Mousavian on Tue, 09/01/2026 - 15:57
Bombing and sanctions have not worked. The US president must seize this moment to establish a comprehensive regional security framework
US President Donald Trump is pictured in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, on 17 August 2026 (Jim Watson/AFP)
On

In recent days, several high-level regional diplomatic initiatives have signalled an effort to revive US-Iran negotiations. 

Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, travelled to Tehran last month, followed by the foreign ministers of Oman and Qatar, each seeking to preserve the Islamabad memorandum of understanding signed by US President Donald Trump and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, in June. 

According to Iranian officials, Tehran delivered a consistent message to all three mediators: Washington should return to the Islamabad memorandum and work towards ending the wars across all regional fronts as the basis for renewed negotiations. 

Yet while Iran and Oman have reached an agreement to open a temporary new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, Washington rejected Tehran’s proposal to return to the Islamabad agreement, and resumed military escalation by striking rocket launchers on Larak Island. 

Iran responded with missile attacks on US bases in Jordan, reinforcing the cycle of confrontation, and signalling that the US remains more committed to coercion than diplomacy.

Eight years ago, Trump abandoned the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, widely regarded as former President Barack Obama’s signature diplomatic legacy. But the Islamabad memorandum is Trump’s own diplomatic legacy.

If Washington is now prepared to walk away from an agreement that bears the signature of its own president, it sends a far broader message: the US is no longer merely abandoning the legacy of previous administrations - it is also abandoning its own. That is a strong indication that Washington has reached the end of its Iran playbook.

Conflicting calculations

Trump’s decision to launch “Economic D-Day” against Iran thus marks a final, decisive economic offensive, which aims to achieve through financial coercion what diplomacy, sanctions, covert action and military force have all failed to accomplish.

The current impasse is sustained not only by conflicting interests, but also by conflicting strategic calculations. 

Washington appears to believe that, after several rounds of military confrontation and the extensive damage inflicted on Iran’s nuclear, missile, military and economic infrastructure, the imposition of the most comprehensive financial and commercial embargo in the history of US-Iran relations will ultimately compel Tehran to accept American terms. 

Tehran appears determined to withstand the current economic offensive and, if necessary, escalate militarily rather than accept another temporary arrangement

This assumption was reflected in recent remarks by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who declared: “We are going to collapse this regime. It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision. You are either with us or against us.”

Tehran’s strategic assessment is markedly different. Based on an analysis I recently heard from an Iranian strategist, Iran’s leadership now views the confrontation with the US as an “existential war” that will shape not only Iran’s future, but also the regional order. 

In this assessment, the Iran war has weakened US military readiness, depleted critical weapons stockpiles, exposed the vulnerability of the global energy system through the Strait of Hormuz, and imposed growing political costs on both Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. 

Consequently, Tehran appears determined to withstand the current economic offensive and, if necessary, escalate militarily rather than accept another temporary arrangement.

Washington might be underestimating the most significant shift in Tehran’s strategic thinking. Many within Iran’s current leadership appear to have reached what Persians describe as “death once, moan once” - a mindset best captured by the English proverb: “A man can die but once.”  

They increasingly believe it is better to resolve the fundamental confrontation with the US once and for all, rather than endure another generation of sanctions, military threats and recurring crises. 

Strategic outlook

The Islamabad memorandum was widely seen in Tehran as a potential turning point, but renewed US military operations, followed by an unprecedented campaign of economic warfare and public calls for regime change, have reinforced the conviction that Washington remains committed to overthrowing the Islamic Republic, regardless of diplomacy. 

This mindset is also reflected in the composition of Iran’s current leadership. The new supreme leader belongs to the generation forged by the Iran-Iraq War, having served as a young soldier on the frontlines. He also carries a legacy of the recent conflict, in which his father, wife and son were killed in US-Israeli military operations. 

Meanwhile, influential figures shaping Iran’s postwar strategy - including parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, and Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei - are veteran commanders of the Iran-Iraq War, whose wartime experiences continue to shape Tehran’s strategic outlook. 

The critical issue is that Washington may now be confronting an Iranian leadership that calculates risk very differently than in years past.

The current crisis has reached what military strategists would describe as a strategic deadlock. Neither Washington nor Tehran possesses a politically acceptable pathway to victory. Although the US can sustain economic warfare far longer than Iran may withstand it economically, such coercion alone is unlikely to achieve Washington’s political objectives or compel Tehran’s surrender.

Iran, meanwhile, retains the ability to impose disproportionate costs on regional stability through maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz, regional military escalation, and disruptions to global energy markets. 

In short, both sides retain the capacity to inflict pain, but neither possesses the ability to impose a durable political settlement by force.

Defining choice

Trump now faces a defining strategic choice. Across his two presidencies, he has left three distinct legacies in US-Iran relations: “maximum pressure”, several military confrontations, and the Islamabad memorandum of understanding. He cannot preserve all three. 

A train cannot run on three different tracks at the same time. If Trump wants history to remember him as the American president who achieved peace with Iran rather than prolonged conflict, he should choose his own diplomatic legacy - the Islamabad memorandum - and transform it into a comprehensive settlement capable of ending nearly five decades of hostility.

Such a grand bargain should concentrate initially on the two issues driving today’s confrontation. The first is the Strait of Hormuz. Rather than allowing the waterway to remain a recurring flashpoint, Washington, Tehran, Muscat and the Arab states in the Gulf should negotiate a permanent maritime security arrangement guaranteeing freedom of navigation, ending maritime confrontation, and recognising the responsibilities of the littoral states under international law. 

Are Iran and the US fighting a war neither side can win?
Read More »

The second is the nuclear issue. Instead of another temporary political understanding vulnerable to changing administrations, both governments should negotiate a bilateral treaty under which Iran would permanently renounce nuclear weapons while preserving its legal and internationally recognised rights to peaceful nuclear technology under the Non-Proliferation Treaty, and the US would permanently remove nuclear-related sanctions. Ratification by both the US Congress and the Iranian parliament would provide a degree of political durability that previous agreements lacked. 

Trump has a rare opportunity to shape a historic legacy. He could help to establish a comprehensive regional security and cooperation framework between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf, transforming one of the world’s most volatile regions into a more stable foundation for global energy security. 

He also has a unique opportunity to facilitate a strategic understanding between Iran and Israel - not necessarily diplomatic normalisation, but a durable arrangement under which both sides would end their mutual military, security and existential threats, replacing “permanent deterrence by crisis” with “stable deterrence by agreement”. 

Such achievements would constitute not merely a diplomatic breakthrough, but a fundamental restructuring of the Middle East’s security architecture - one with lasting benefits for regional stability, global commerce and American strategic interests.

title: The world banned landmines and cluster munitions. Can it stop killer AI before it is too late?
summary:
The world banned landmines and cluster munitions. Can it stop killer AI before it is too late?

Submitted by Gergana Krasteva on Wed, 09/02/2026 - 08:13
Campaigners race to rein in systems ‘designed to kill’, as autonomous weapons lower the threshold for war and increase civilian harm
A plume of smoke rises after a strike on the Iranian capital Tehran, on 3 March 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off

Throughout the history of war, the machinery of killing has always left room for a human to intervene.

A soldier could see the person in front of them and choose to maim rather than kill; a pilot could identify the target, question the intelligence and decide not to strike.

Technology has been steadily changing that. Autonomous weapons systems now threaten to remove any meaningful human control over the use of force in conflict.

AI-assisted targeting was first deployed by Israel in its genocidal war on Gaza and then in Iran, with strikes happening at unprecedented speed - over 1,000 hits in the first 24 hours of the US-Israeli war, suggesting the use of automated systems.

For more than 13 years, the global coalition Stop Killer Robots has been fighting to prevent that future, pushing governments towards a ban on machines capable of selecting and engaging targets without oversight.

“The systems are designed to kill, so there are no checks and balances anymore,” executive director Nicole van Rooijen told Middle East Eye.

“If a system is designed to kill, it will kill, right? And that in itself is problematic as it is very much contingent on the type of information that is fed into the machine.”

Van Rooijen pointed to the US air strike on Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the Iranian city of Minab on 28 February, in which 156 people, including 120 children, were killed, as an example.

Evidence indicates that US forces hit the building, located next to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) compound. To this day, that attack is the deadliest throughout the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Inaccuracy that kills

“Preliminary information is that it is a US strike, but also that it is due to outdated intelligence fed into the machine,” Van Roijen said.

“If the information is not completely accurate or is outdated, it has devastating consequences on the ground, most likely for innocent civilians.

‘It is false promises of being more accurate, more precise, yet the results are worse, not for their militaries but for civilians on the ground. They pay the brunt of it’

- Nicole van Roijen, executive director of Stop Killer Robots

“This is especially true in a volatile environment when you are conducting hostilities but you do not have boots on the ground to confirm what the machine wants to target.”

Another major issue is accuracy. Specialists working on AI and integration into the military kill chain have estimated reliability at between 25 and 50 percent, Van Rooijen explained.

“And that is the best-case scenario,” she added. “The analogy is carpet bombing.”

Stop Killer Robots have also sounded the alarm that autonomous weapons systems “drastically” lower the threshold for going to war as it does not require deploying a military force.

“No one wants to see their soldiers die on foreign land, so that calls for some restraint. You think twice about sending your own people,” Van Rooijen.

“If it is all automated, you can just send machines. Israel and the US have been threatening Iran for decades, but never actually went through with it, and I do not think it is a coincidence… it gives you a false sense that you can do it quickly… and come back a winner.

“But it is false promises of being more accurate, more precise, yet the results are worse, not for their militaries but for civilians on the ground. They pay the brunt of it.”

No guardrail

Currently, there is no common, agreed upon definition of what an autonomous system is.

There is no treaty that regulates how they are being developed, tested, sold or deployed, setting up the conditions for a “free for all” arms race for tech giants to make a fortune “out of the misery of people”, Van Roijen said.

She finds the absence of protections particularly difficult to reconcile.

‘An autonomous weapon system is a machine and a machine cannot truly understand the value of a human life’

- Bonnie Docherty, senior arms advisor at HRW

“There are more guardrails in place if you test a new airplane, or a new car, than integrating AI into the kill chain,” she noted.

Looking back in history, there is a precedent for stopping a weapon before governments can no longer imagine warfare without it.

Among those campaigning for a treaty governing autonomous weapons systems is senior arms advisor at Human Rights Watch (HRW), Bonnie Docherty, who had a central role in the negotiations that eventually led to the 2008 Convention on Cluster Munitions, which prohibited their use.

She told Middle East Eye that the fight over autonomous weapons systems follows the same principles of humanitarian disarmament, striving to prevent arms-inflicted human sufferings.

For Docherty, boiling down individuals to numbers, and “delegating life and death decisions” to machines, is a “great concern”.

“An autonomous weapon system is a machine and a machine cannot truly understand the value of a human life,” she explained.

“To give that machine the power to kill… is ethically inappropriate. Whoever is taking a life should be able to understand the significance of it.”

Deja vu

Evidence gathered by HRW additionally shows that systems can reproduce or amplify algorithm biases, which can be lethal.

“We looked at the discrimination front and particularly at race, gender and disability,” she said. “For example, on the disability front, artificial intelligence may have trouble distinguishing a cane from a gun.”

Israel using AI weapons system co-produced with Indian firm in war on Gaza
Read More »

Yet states like the US, Israel, Russia and China are reluctant to surrender weapons that could give them an advantage, a hackneyed argument that Docherty knows too well. Behind them is also a tech industry peddling its own commercial incentives.

She has heard it before, in the negotiations over the cluster munitions treaty. Governments were greedy to retain technologies they were developing, arguing that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient.

What broke the camel’s back at the time, as Doherty put it, was Israel's blanket deployment of cluster munition strikes in southern Lebanon in 2006. Many submunitions remain scattered across the territory to this day, resulting in hundreds of deaths and injuries.

“I feel like I am having a deja vu,” Docherty said. “A lot of these arguments, you could just plug in the same weapons system.”

Last week, the United Nations secretary-general and the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) renewed their call for a treaty governing autonomous weapons systems.

Three years earlier, they had urged states to establish rules by 2026. Now that the deadline has become “untenable”, they warned that the world is fast approaching a “moral red line”.

The renewed appeal also comes as the ICRC suspects that increasingly sophisticated forms of autonomy are being integrated into weapons systems across a range of conflicts, not only into defensive but also offensive operations, including in populated areas.

Legal adviser with the ICRC, Georgia Hinds, told Middle East Eye: “While it is very hard for us to verify… we are seeing this increasing integration of autonomy into weapons in many conflicts, from sophisticated military capabilities down to more commercial off-the-shelf systems that are being adapted.”

‘A big risk’

What the organisation is insistent about is that there is still hope in the form of a diplomatic route to negotiate the rules around the systems.

In November, states will gather in Geneva for the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), which takes place every five years.

‘It is also likely to be used by non-state actors who fall outside of those more regulated investigation mechanisms’

- Georgia Hinds, legal adviser at the ICRC

It could be a watershed moment for the campaign as the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems, the primary UN intergovernmental forum addressing emerging technologies related to autonomous weapons, has been developing a draft text, which includes prohibitions on some systems and restrictions on others.

The final session of the group takes place this week, and its work will then feed into the upcoming conference.

Campaigners are hoping that it could be turned into formal negotiations for a legally binding treaty - at last.

“It really would not take much now to convert that into a binding instrument,” Hinds said. “In November, the decision needs to be taken to move to formal negotiations.

Rights groups call for a halt of AI tech use in the military
Read More »

“Rolling over discussions that have now been ongoing for nearly 13 years in the group of governmental experts is not acceptable. There is really only one option in November for us.”

If states do agree, a treaty could be only months away. The preferred - and shortest - route would be to masterfully negotiate an additional protocol under the CCW.

However, experts like Hinds are doubtful as to how realistic this is. She said that the conference does not offer a simple yes-or-no ending, and that there are several ways to progress with the campaign.

The overall goal is to get ahead of the technology, she added, warning that as autonomous weapons spread, it becomes easier for anyone - even armed groups outside any legal oversight - to turn cheap commercial tech into deadly autonomous weapons.

“The [more] opportunity for these systems to proliferate, the easier it becomes to adapt a commercially available system… it is also likely to be used by non-state actors who fall outside of those more regulated investigation mechanisms,” Hinds said.

“All of these things again increase accountability concerns for me. So yes, I think it's a big risk.”

[…]

The reporting also linked a 2024 Department No. 4 graduate, Aleksei Kondrashov, to Military Unit 74455, widely known as Sandworm.

That unit has been associated with destructive cyber activity against Ukraine and other targets, including the 2017 NotPetya attack.

The reports do not establish that every listed graduate participated in a named operation; assignments should therefore be described as reported unit placements, not proof of individual operational involvement...

title: Response to US attacks will be 'extensive and widespread', Iranian army warns
summary:
Response to US attacks will be 'extensive and widespread', Iranian army warns

The Iranian army has claimed attacks on radar systems, operational centres and areas sheltering US forces in Bahrain and the UAE.

In a statement it said that Washington's targeting of residential areas and a wedding in Iran is a "clear example of a war crime and reveals the vile nature of 'American human rights'".

"The army's response to these crimes will certainly be extensive and widespread."

title: Kuwait says fire 'under control' after Iranian attacks, as IRGC claims strikes on US facilities
summary:
Kuwait says fire 'under control' after Iranian attacks, as IRGC claims strikes on US facilities

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it attacked several bases across the region, including the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, where it claimed it "killed a number of enemy elements".

In a statement, the IRGC said it carried out a combined missile and drone attack on the military base in Kuwait hosting US forces, adding that it targeted the headquarters and residence of the American commander of the base. 

It added that the attack destroyed several US drones and set fire to a drone hangar and a ramp through which UAVs participated in strikes on Iran.

"What is painful and worrying for us is the occupation of Islamic lands by the child-killing and terrorist army of America," the IRGC said. 

"These attacks are to help you cleanse the pure land and homeland of the righteous, Kuwait, from the filth of the American infidels."

Meanwhile, Kuwait's official KUNA news agency said that an Iranian drone attack caused a fire in a residential complex.

"A fire that broke out in a residential complex in the Capital Governorate has been brought under control. The complex had been targeted by a hostile drone launched as part of the nefarious Iranian aggression," a fire department spokesperson was quoted as saying, adding there were no casualties.

title: Israeli army says earlier interception likely 'false target'
summary:
Israeli army says earlier interception likely 'false target'

The Israeli military said that its interception of a "suspicious aerial target" was "apparently launched at a false target".

Earlier, the army announced that "interceptors were launched toward a suspicious aerial target," alleging that it crossed from Lebanese territory into northern Israel.

title: Morning update
summary:
Morning update

Good morning, Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • The US military announced on Tuesday that it has completed fresh attacks on Iran, with local reports indicating that civilians attending a wedding were amongst the latest victims. In response, Tehran carried out strikes across the region on US facilities and its troops, including in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Iraq's northern Kurdish province of Erbil.

  • The spokesperson of Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warned that operations against the US will "continue as a lesson to them until they regret their crime". He warned that the continuation of "American evil in the region will be met with heavier, broader, and more devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences".

  • US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said that 17 million barrels of oil transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. Wright's statement shows a discrepancy with preliminary ship-tracking data from Kpler, which recorded only five commodity vessels transiting the waterway that day, with no liquid tankers recorded.

  • US President Donald Trump has denied reports alleging that he is trying to bring Iran back into peace discussions. "I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table, as ABC Fake News reported. I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement," he said in a post on his platform Truth Social. He added that the US has "almost total control" over the Hormuz Strait.

  • Two Israeli air strikes targeted the vicinity of the southern Lebanese towns of Kfar Rumman and Arab Salim in southern Lebanon, Al Jazeera reported. A short while before, the Israeli army announced that "interceptors were launched toward a suspicious aerial target" that it alleged crossed from Lebanese territory into northern Israel.
